utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin to hear evidence of this witness, there are -- seem -- there seem to be several administrative matters. Yes, Mr. Tieger, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning. And good morning, Your Honours. I wanted to raise two quick matters. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll -- yes, we'll wait till we hear from you, Mr. Tieger. Today we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We had some technical difficulties which seems to be resolved by now. I was telling the parties that we are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Flavia Lattanzi sitting in other case. And there's one issue as to which the Chamber is going to issue an oral ruling by Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now issue an oral decision on the accused's 69th motion for finding of disclosure violation and for sanctions, February the -- of 2012, filed on the 29th of February, 2012, alleging a violation by the Prosecution of Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence for the delayed disclosure of a two-page statement of 92 bis Witness KDZ186. The Prosecution filed its response to the motion on the 14th of March, 2012. The Chamber, having reviewed the statement and considering the Prosecution's acknowledgment that it should have been disclosed by the 7th of May, 2009, deadline for disclosure of such material, finds that the Prosecution violated its disclosure obligations pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii) by only disclosing the statement on the 21st of February, 2012. While the Prosecution violated its disclosure obligation, the Chamber finds that the accused suffered no prejudice as a result of the late disclosure of this single two-page statement of KDZ186. In reaching that conclusion, the Chamber reviewed the statement and found that it was not of such significance that its late disclosure resulted in any prejudice to the accused. In that regard, the Chamber notes that the accused did not allege, and failed to demonstrate, that he had been prejudiced in any way by this late disclosure. In the absence of demonstrated prejudice, there is no basis to grant the accused's request that KDZ186's evidence be excluded. For these reasons, the Chamber grants, by majority, Judge Kwon dissenting, the motion in part and finds that the Prosecution violated Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules with respect to the late disclosure of the statement and denies the motion in all other respects. Judge Kwon refers to his partially dissenting opinion in the decision on the accused's 37th to 42nd disclosure violation motions with partially dissenting opinion of Judge Kwon, 29th of March, 2011. While Judge Kwon agrees with the majority that there has been a violation of Rule 66(A)(ii) of the Rules, in the absence of prejudice to the accused, he considers that the motion should be dismissed in its entirety. The Chamber takes this opportunity to clarify that its previous instruction in its decision on the accused's 32nd, 33rd, 35th, and 36th disclosure violation motions filed on the 24th of February, 2011, that "unless a disclosure violation motion seeks an urgent remedy, the resources of all parties, including the Defence and the Chamber, would be better served if the accused filed a consolidated disclosure violation motion on a monthly basis." It is not an invitation to automatically file a disclosure motion ever month, as in this case there is such limited material and there is no allegation of prejudice and no urgent remedies sought. The Chamber invites the accused and his legal advisors to focus their energy and resources on motions which raise significant issues and to consider the utility of filing motions which make no allegation of prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the completion of French translation. My apologies, Mr. Witness, for your inconvenience. If the witness take the -- I'm sorry. If the witness could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: KDZ245

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Without reading out loud, do you see in front of you a document, and do you see the name on it? Is it -- that your name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4594, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. May I please now have 65 ter 90317.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, while the document is going to come up on your screen, I first would like to ask you: Is that correct that you gave a statement to the Prosecution in 1999 and then you subsequently testified in three cases: in the Krstic case in 2001, in the Popovic case in 2006, and in the Tolimir case in 2010; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And an amalgamated statement was prepared containing the relevant portion of your previous testimonies and interview. And, Witness, do you see that statement on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I see what I see, and I see my signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. So is this the document that, as you can see from the date, you signed a few days ago on the 9th of March?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this document read to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: KDZ245

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question on this. Sir, if you were asked today about the same matter, would you provide this Court the same information that are contained in the statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I think I would provide the very same information. I don't know what else I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this statement and also 24 associated exhibits. And I should indicate that contrary to what we indicate in our final associated exhibit list, we do not tender two of the three handwritten notebooks. In particular, we would not tender 65 ter 35006 and 35020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you are tendering 35027?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to 35027, the notebook, we would ask that only the intercepts contained in the notebook that are referred to by the witness be admitted, as opposed to the entire notebook themselves. If there's some page that is necessary to also include to show the date of the intercept, we don't have any objection to that. With respect to the intercepts themselves, we would ask the Chamber to wait until it hears the cross-examination before making a decision about the admissibility of those, although we may not oppose them by the time the cross-examination is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the second part of your submission, Mr. Robinson. These intercepts are tendered as part of associated exhibit, following his 92 ter statement. But why do we have to wait till we hear cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you're just admitting them for the limited purpose of understanding his testimony, then, of course, you can do that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the intercepts themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Individual intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, it's true that they make -- they constitute a part of his statement and you can admit them on that basis, but the whole exercise here is to determine the reliability of the intercepts. So if you're going to admit them for that basis, I think you ought to hear the cross-examination first. For example, let's say the witness included in his statement: My colleagues and I -- I've seen 65 ter number 1, my colleagues and I wrote this up as a joke and so it's not reliable. That could be admissible as part of a -- an integral part of his statement but may not -- would not be admissible as a reliable intercept. So I think you ought to at least wait until you hear the cross-examination before making a determination about admissibility of an intercept on the basis of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Costi, can I hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you, Mr. President. As for the notebooks, we would -- we seeked admission of the notebook not -- not as much for the content of the notebook itself but we do believe that having a full notebook, at least one, would assist the Chamber in assessing the whole intercepting process. So we do think it would be of -- of help to the Chamber in their determination of the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we shop here for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, for that limited purpose I take it you don't object to the admission of that notebook, handwritten notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And as for the second matter, it seems to be a -- I understand my friend Robinson's raised a potential reliability issue. We would submit that at this stage the 89(C) standard has been met through the statement of the witness who has recognised the intercept itself, who has discussed in details the process through which this intercept were taken, and who has described the reliability and the carefulness they applied in this process. So if we look at the standard of Rule 89(C), which is a prima facie standard and not a beyond reasonable doubt standard, we believe the standard at this stage is met and there is no reason not to admit this intercept. Now, obviously, if at the end of the cross-examination, and even later, in light of the totality of the evidence when assessing the weight of this intercept Your Honour were to decide that they are unreliable or you want -- you don't want to give any weight to it, then, of course, this is part of your final assessment and determination of the evidence. So in my submission this evidence should be admitted now, and, of course, Your Honour will have to assess at the end of the case the weight to give to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from these intercepts included in -- in this associated exhibit list, was there some Srebrenica intercepts that may be potentially authenticated by these witnesses? And are you going to deal with them now, or what is your plan for those intercepts that have been marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We believe that the testimonies of this witness and the next witness as well as to the process goes to the authenticity of intercepts taken by the same organs to which our witness is part of. We -- our plan more in general for the other intercept related to Srebrenica is to file as soon as possible a comprehensive motion where we will explain 89(C), why they met the 89(C) standard in terms of reliability and probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this witness will testify to the authenticity of those intercepts. So just -- I'm speaking for myself, from the top of my head, how about marking for identification all the intercepts and then we deal with it all together, because we need -- we may need some witnesses to give some context.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be unclear and imprecise actually. This witness, we believe, will authenticate the specific intercept discussed in his statement. As for the other exhibit, we believe that will be -- we will submit they should be taken -- that there should be judicial notice of their authenticity pursuant to Rule 94, if I'm not wrong. My point was that his testimony in general about the process, we will submit in our motion, to some extent supports previous determination of other Chambers as to the authenticity of all the intercepts taken by the ABiH in the Srebrenica area. So as far as the specific authentification [sic] of this -- of this witness concern, I would say that it refers specifically to the intercept we're going to discuss today, and that's why I would submit that they should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consult -- the Chamber will consult the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this case we'll grant the Defence request to wait till the end of the cross-examination and see what we can do at the time. Otherwise, all the other exhibits, associated exhibits, will be admitted and be given number in due course by the Registry. Yes, Mr. Costi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now I would like to read a short summary of the witness testimony. During the war, the witness served as a member of an intercept unit of the ABiH. He was assigned to the so-called southern facility, which he contributed to establish. The southern facility was an elevation with no natural obstacles. It was a prime location for listening to the VRS communication in the Srebrenica area. His task and the task of his unit was to intercept the radio relay communication of the VRS. The witness's testimonies describe the equipment they used, as well as the process of intercepting, recording, transcribing all the relevant conversations. And as for the process, the witness testified that first an order from the command would indicate the frequencies and direction to monitor, that's because the command had a complete picture and was in a position to determine the direction of the interesting information. The witness would then scan the required frequencies and when you heard a sound, we stopped the scanner and start recording the conversation. The conversation considered relevant would then be transcribed on a working notebook. The witness and his unit made sure that the transcription was accurate and if something was not recognizable, they wouldn't guess. They would write that it was an inaudible part. And, similarly, if the speaker was not identified, they would write a number or sign instead. Finally, the notebook, the working notebook we are talking about, was passed over to typists and a typist who would type the conversation in a computer. They would then encrypt and send information to the command. The witness explained that no editing was made in the process of typing the information into the computer. The witness recognised his handwriting on several pages and discussed in detail three intercept conversations relevant to this case. And he recalls that when he heard one of these conversation, he realized that there was a hunt for men. And this, Your Honour, would end my summary. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I have very few questions for the witness, but could we please go in private session for the first question I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber -- yes, we are now in open session. But give me a minute, Mr. Costi. Could we move back to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your statement you gave us the details of the process you followed in intercepting and transcribing these conversations. I would like to just briefly and in simple terms describe the Trial Chamber which were the steps that you took from the order you received to the typed version.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, look, first of all, if there was something we were to listen to and to transcribe, then on the other side there had to be two radios in a network which made it possible to use phone lines, because phone lines were used up until the 1990s. So this is now outdated. But the Army of Yugoslavia and the VRS used this system. At our work posts, we had something that we called a combination, which included a number of devices, and this enabled us to listen to the communications over this radio relay link, and we did this by using this basic device. A radio relay has 24 channels, so it was possible to scan all 24 channels, because the operator who worked in our central station, 1.800, could follow any channel, so in one central you could follow 24 channels and the conversation between participants. In the combination that we used, we had a device that could memorize a certain number for all those 24 channels, and those channels or frequencies could then be scanned. The device was such that you could adjust its speed. So in only a few seconds, all 24 channels would be activated. And then an operator monitoring communications when a signal appeared, a very brief one, it was a tone, a sound of some kind, so when this sound was heard, the scanning would stop immediately. Then you'd have to go two or three channels back. And from that point in time, when you hear that you have found something, you press a button on the record -- on the tape recorder, and then the conversation is recorded on the tape. When the conversation is finished, the operator turns it off. And then depending on how urgent the matter is, sometimes it was urgent to send what had been intercepted to a command, but depending on the urgency, the operator would have someone else transcribe the conversation into these log-books, for example, that are in evidence here. Then the operator would transcribe the conversation that had been recorded. The Prosecutor has already said that when something wasn't clear to us, when we didn't understanding something correctly, we didn't arbitrarily interpret what it was. So we just make a note of the fact that it was inaudible or that it couldn't be understood. So we accurately reflected the recorded conversation. We accurately transcribed it in the notebook. Sometimes, after a shift, an operator would make entries. We had an operator who liked to use computers for transcription purposes. So sometimes an operator would type the text from the notebook into a computer. And then the text would be forwarded by a Paket communications to the command or the forward command post, and so on and so forth. It all depended on which matters were urgent, priority matters. So that is the basic manner in which we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just the last question for you: Have you ever been or ever been deployed to the other intercept facility, the so-called northern facility?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of November, 1995. Action had come to an end, more or less, at the time, and then the whole unit moved from the southern facility to the northern facility where we joined the staff of the northern facility. And that's where we were when the war ended in 1996. We left that area in 1996. At least I did. However, some people stayed on there afterwards, and I don't know when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And for what you could see when you were there, would you say that the protocol, the procedure adopted for intercepting communication, was, let's say, similar, if not the same, of the one you previously adopted during the war at the southern facility?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. The procedure followed was, one could say, identical, as we were part of the same unit, as the same command structure. We had the same company commander. So, in general, everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would end my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in this case, your examination-in-chief, or evidence in-chief, was admitted in lieu of your oral testimony in a written form. Now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed, did you not, that you served in the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. Should I say when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. But you served in the JNA. And which branch?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I was in the communications department, a radio telegram operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you inherit some sort of equipment when the war broke out? Did any equipment fall into your hands, and did you have the same equipment that the other side had?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, we did inherit something at the southern facility, but only antennae. As for everything else, well, the equipment you have in mind, well, with that equipment, that military equipment, we couldn't have done anything, so it wasn't necessary for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of equipment did you use for your work?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, the equipment we used was equipment produced by international producers such as Icom, Kenwood, Yaesu. We had receivers, Icom receivers. AOR receivers. We had these basic Kenwood units, these 450 devices. We had UHER recorders that were used by organisations for their sessions, their work council sessions, for example, and by other reporters at radio stations for the public in general. And we also had a small device called a balance mixer. That was a key element for receiving the signal we were interested in. And that is a device that was invented a long time ago. I didn't invent it, nor we didn't invent it. But some of the devices I myself created, constructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. But since we're speaking the same language, please wait for the transcript to come to an end. Then you can speak.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, where was this equipment from? The equipment that wasn't inherited from the JNA, where did you obtain it from and when?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Much of the equipment was obtained from the radio clubs that existed at the time. So, for example, we obtained equipment from my radio club. All the equipment from that club. But many devices were provided through channels I'm not aware of. From various places in the world. I don't really know how it was obtained. All I know is what sort of equipment we had on-site and what sort of equipment we actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was equipment that was more modern. It was newer than the equipment you had inherited.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: We only inherited antennas. We had to construct quite a few antennas too, but all the other equipment was more modern than the radio relay equipment that the Yugoslav army used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your equipment was more modern than the equipment that the VRS had?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I'm only talking about radio relay equipment used for communications. I'm not talking about other radio relay equipment. I don't know what the other side had, and I wouldn't like to express an opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me, were these systems compatible? The systems that the two or three warring factions had, were they compatible with each other?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, in certain cases, yes, when it came to ordinary radio communications for which the usual frequencies were used. In our system, in various municipalities, for example, the same radio relay communication system was used. But when we talk about interceptions and so on, I don't think that this was the case, because our units didn't have radio relay communications that were established in such ways. They had this particular system of communications which was more encrypted, which was a safer system, in comparison to the system that the VRS had for which these radio relay devices were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these various communications systems result in sound distortion? Did they affect the quality of the sound? Was there any interference as a result of this, of the systems used?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: When the signal was heard, it was usually quite distinct. With the exception of certain words. For example, we had some of these devices for communications between our commands, and when the device starts omitting a signal, you can usually hear it in your headphones. And that signal can affect the audibility of a certain word and then we make a note of the fact. But since -- if you have two radio relay communication devices, if they're to communicate with each other, there has to be optical visibility. In other words, the antenna of one radio relay had to be matched with the signal of the other radio relay, and then we capture the signal from somewhere else. Sometimes we could hear only one radio relay station and not the other one, and then we would draw the conclusion that one participant could be heard and not the other one. But when you go through our log-books, you can see whether we could hear one of the participants, several of the participants, both participants, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also intercept the conversations of the third warring party?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Since we were far away, I didn't, or, rather, my unit did didn't do that at our facility. As for whether anyone did anything within the third warring faction, I don't know. We only intercepted conversations of the Drina Corps. That's the area from Bijeljina and all the way up to Cajnici [phoen]. That's the area concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we establish the purpose for which this was done in fact? Am I right if I say that the command issued an order for these interceptions and this was in order to inform the command of the intentions of the other side, of what was going on on the other side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, the unit that I was a member of was established for that purpose, because, Mr. Karadzic, we intercepted the conversations you had, and we intercepted the conversations of your generals and high-ranking officers. So we intercepted conversations at that level alone. We weren't interested in lower-level conversations. Other people would intercept such conversations by using different devices and a different technical system. So we intercepted the conversations that your cabinet had, conversations that Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic had, Mladic's, Tutaric's [phoen] conversations, and so on and so forth. I won't list all the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to pause and wait for interpretation. So it served the sole purpose of informing your commanders. There was no other purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did a court participate in the process of decision-making by way of issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Did someone provide orders to my command? I don't know. I only knew what my superior requested me to do, and I organised the work around that task and performed it as an officer. I'm not familiar with any other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I can see that many tapes were destroyed, did anyone warn you that you should preserve them, as they might be used in courts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, you see, never, throughout the war, did I think I would attend a court such as this one to testify. We did that for the purpose of our defence, and that's how I saw my job. I can tell you that until May or June 1994 all such material, such as the notebooks, was destroyed, burned. We didn't even think that they might be used for anything else. As for the tapes, once a tape ended and shifts rotated, we handed them over. It was usually the company commander who did that. Or the next company commander would receive it, the full tape, and take it to the command. Then we would be told to erase the tape or perhaps listen to a particular conversation again. But, for the most part, they were erased and then returned to us to be used again. I don't know whether before erasing them they were copied onto some other tapes. That is something I don't know. But I do know that there's very little material that was recorded before the summer of 1994 that was preserved, although it contained important matters such as the events of winter 1993. It would be very interesting to have it, in particular, in a forum such as this one. But we never thought that it might come in handy before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that before the notebooks were kept, everything was written down on sheets of paper which were not kept, they were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. At least in my unit. I don't know about the other locations. But when there was a certain amount of such material, we simply burned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I noticed that tapes were hardly ever numbered and filed in a particular way.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I think they weren't, actually. If there are numbers on the tapes, these are probably numbers that different companies assigned to these tapes, because these tapes were used for workers' council sessions or something like that. But I didn't really notice anything like that. I didn't really pay any attention to it either because that wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, a tape was not marked in a way so as to make it clear where it was in the notebook. So it wasn't really matched to the notebook markings.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: No. Because, for example, a notebook might be filled up before a tape. And then it could happen that a tape could still remain in the facility even when the notebook would be full and sent off elsewhere. In principle, the tape and notebook were only used by us as work material to create a file or a report in our computer to say what it was that was recorded. So then in the computer there would be the date, the number of the document, and so on, and which area was being listened to, and so on. And very often you cannot find that in notebooks. Because these notebooks were really like the papers that we destroyed until 1994. This was just working material for us. We did not see any linkage. We did not really link [Realtime transcript read in error "like"] these things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you known that it would be used somewhere before a court of law, what was supposed to have been done in order to make things better? What are the things that you did not do because you did not have a court of law in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence: [In English] "... did not really like ..." Instead: "... did not really link ..." [Interpretation] This is mistyped in the last line. The witness said: "We did not really link these things up," and the transcript says "We did not really like these things up." Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Are you referring to my last answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that "I did not link things up." You didn't talk about me liking something. The tape and the notebook.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, we didn't link these things up because this was simply working material for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you know that you are in this situation, tell us: What were the things that should have been done in order to have made things better, or different?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just wonder: The witness is not a lawyer, so I'm not sure he can answer this sort of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Costi. Mr. Karadzic, he answered the question. He -- he didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, if he's thinking now, it would be useful if we would know. Perhaps we could link things up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for you to make submission later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did it sometimes happen that a conversation would not be recorded but, rather, taken down live, written up as it was taking place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that, as far as these intercepts are concerned, if something was omitted, it would usually be the very beginning of the communication taking place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: If you understood what I said in the beginning, what I said at the beginning of my testimony, I said that permanently 24 channels were listened to and then what can happen is the following: For example, the scanner gets to this particular channel and then a speaker is silent for some reason and then the other channels have to go through and then sometimes the conversations did not really start from the beginning. And then we have to go two or three channels back if there was this silence, so there's always this possibility of part of a conversation not being recorded. But usually it's two operators who are establishing the link, so it didn't really affect things much. Usually in the beginning there would be an exchange of greetings and things like that. So then later on, from the moment when the conversation was recorded, it would be written down in the notebook. We did not write anything before that. For example, if we knew which radio devices these were and then we'd say "Badem" and another code-name -- well. Just so that one would know which radio relay communication it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, did this create problems for you, in terms of identification? Because, at the very beginning of the conversation, usually the participants in the conversation identify each other and greet each other by using each other's names. Did you have to make a special effort to identify them if you do not hear their names?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Just a moment. If we would not hear their names, we never tried to write down some name or invent some name unless we were 100 per cent sure. We knew the voices of quite a few officers. For example, when I talked to my friends or if a friend calls me, I don't really have to think who it is. I recognise their voices. So then we used to recognise a lot of these voices, and then we'd write down "Krstic," "Popovic," whoever, I mean, the persons whose voices we would recognised, and then if not, usually we'd mark the interlocutors by numbers - 1, 2, 3 - depending on how many interlocutors were involved. So if we were not 100 per cent sure that we knew who it was, then we would not guess in any way that this was this person or that person or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the issuers of your transcripts. Did the identity of the participants really matter to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, it mattered to us, too. It was interesting to know who it was that was talking. And certainly it was of interest to my superiors too. Often when I'd finish my shift I would go to my command, to my superiors, and then I'd see on the wall some of these work maps, operation maps, where they would mark code-names - Milici, Vlasenica, Zvornik. Each unit had its own code-name. And then I saw that from these transcripts of ours, next to every one of these code-names they would write up the names of the officers, roughly, and whatever else was heard in the conversations. So the command new roughly which team of officers belonged to a particular unit, worked in a particular unit. That's what I saw. But I really had nothing to do with that because we did not specifically deal with that particular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just so you know, I'm waiting for the interpretation. You mentioned that you underwent training. This was probably in the JNA. What did it include, this training?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: In the JNA, from May -- March 1967 until 1968, I was in a radio telegraph unit where we learned the Morse code, because the then-army used that system a lot. Radio telegraphy, in addition to teleprinters and so on and so forth. I, since I was a top-notch operator even before the war and I had taken all these exams, not a single one of our trainers was better than I was, so I assisted them. Once we underwent certain training, once people learned certain things, then communications would be established. That kind of practice was carried out, how to use this system. Even before I came to do my military service in the army I had had tens of thousands of communications throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can discuss that in public, can we not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this needs to be redacted. Although I personally think that it's not really necessary, because there are a lot of ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: A lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this training involve some kind of voice recognition training, some kind of music training, if I can call it that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: When I was in the JNA, there was also a unit that dealt with radiophony. Now, whether they had something along those lines, I don't know. Because the Morse code is a completely different type of communication where there are no voices. There is this monotonous tone that is heard as a signal, like when you're pressing that button. There's really nothing to -- I mean, it's important to understand the code, the combination of those two signs, and then you would know what each letter was. And that is how text could be encoded and decoded and then written up in hand, so -- I don't know. I didn't undergo any such training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is no metacommunication. There is no irony. There are no jokes. Everything is literal in Morse code; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: You're right. Exactly. Tit, ta, that's the way it is. Dot, hyphen. Everything is monotonous. There are no oscillations in tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Weather conditions and the electromagnetic situation, did they affect the quality of the sound that was recorded and heard?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Only if there was a lot of thunder. Then that could be heard in the headphones. Nothing else affected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that - actually, you spoke about this - that you were never ordered to identify the interlocutors involved?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I don't recall any order that arrived. I mean, whatever we heard, we wrote down. If we knew who the interlocutor was, then we'd write down who it was. And if we did not know, then we'd give numbers. Interlocutor 1, Interlocutor 2, 3, 4, and so on. And then in that way we would state who it was that was actually talking. We thought that that was the only right thing to do. I don't remember that anyone ever asked us to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you notice that there was a lot of metacommunication involved, something that cannot be read but it can be felt if you're just listening? Irony, self-irony, jokes, exaggerations. Did you notice that speech is full of that, as opposed to the written word?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: There were situations when sometimes the interlocutors would curse, swear, make jokes. We did not take that into account. Our notebooks reflected everything that was said in the original. I don't think that we stated if they laughed or things like that. Or at least I didn't do anything like that. So it was just normal. I mean, when people talk, that kind of thing happens as well. It depends on how close they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there are Serbs and Croats and Muslims there. And they're rather similar, if not the same. Do we agree that quite a few proverbs are used, figures of speech, allusions, and so on, when we speak? Were you in a position to observe that, and did you notify the users of your transcripts of that as part of this metacommunication, as part of this figurative speech?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: As I've already said, we wrote down in our notebooks only what it was that we heard. We never went into giving any kind of comment with regard to anyone's conversation or any conversation. There were civilian conversations as well, because many officers talked to their wives, families, friends, and so on. We sent those conversations on as well, but they probably ended up only in the notebook and the command. So it was only what we heard. We never went into any kind of comments of our own regarding anything, except for what had been recorded and conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I to understand, then, that the user of your transcript, the commander, could only read what was written down, without any additional instructions, notes, or remarks that this or that was a joke or an exaggeration, allusion, or a turn of phrase?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: As regards my facility, I don't think we ever did that. We only forwarded what had been recorded. No comments were made. Never. That was not our job, and no one asked us to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the commanders receiving only transcripts, without listening to the conversations you recorded and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: When once we have recorded a conversation, we transcribed it into a notebook, and that text from the notebook was typed into the computer in its totality. And then through the digital repeater communication links the operator forwarded such messages, and no other people were involved, save for the operators themselves. On the sending end, it was encrypted and decrypted at the other end and then sent to the person who was supposed to receive it. The tapes themselves were retained to some extent and then people could check things. I don't know whether it was done or not. And once by the time the tape has arrived, the information contained on it was already too old and not up to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was interested in how they would interpret this sentence. Were there any omissions or mistakes that were made, and were you ever requested to correct them by your command? When I say "omissions or mistakes," I have in mind the handling of all that material, as well as in the way you kept the notes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I have to repeat yet again. Once a text had been transcribed and noted down in the notebook, it was typed into the computer in the very same form, and sent. Which meant our job was done. We never received any information where it was requested that we checked or corrected something. Our superiors knew how we worked. If we had not done our job properly before sending it -- well, sometimes if there was an important conversation and we couldn't hear or make something out, everyone who was in that shift came and listened to that particular conversation. Only when everyone agreed that it was inaudible, we made that note, and there was no need to carry out any further checks or corrections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, could we see 05207.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, my previous question was aimed more at the pattern, standard procedure of note-taking that was in place. Could you have a look at this document for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe it may be broadcast. 1D05207. That's not quite the thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is it. Could we have it in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this captain who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We now zoom -- I'm sorry. We'll not broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that it says something about the forwarding of the report to the PEB?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I can't find it right away, but I know what PEB stands for. That was the name of our unit, counter-electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where it says RRPC, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Radio relay interception something. I'm not quite familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to make sure, I wouldn't mention the name of the centre, if you were asked to -- if the witness is asked to read the document, he should be careful not to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I told not to broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't do that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that it has to do with certain shortcomings and deficiencies which need to be corrected for the purpose of ensuring the maximum quality of radio monitoring information. And then we have the order itself. This is in August, late August 1995. So in item 1 (a) the following is requested. The original conversation is being forwarded as recorded. And then we have the specific information. Then, under item 2, we have scrambling. Well, what prompted the command that they should request the conversations to be forwarded literally as they had been recorded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: You mentioned scrambling. We didn't engage in that. And this was probably not send to us. I don't recall any such thing. This was the scrambling unit. I don't know what they worked on, and perhaps they were not doing their job sufficiently well and they were cautioned. You yourself said it concerned scrambling, which had nothing to do with my unit. It would have been counter-productive for us who were trying to listen in to scramble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree that item 2 has to do with scrambling, but look at item 1. There they ask that any conversations that are forwarded need to be recorded literally. It only means that they had a sufficient reason to make that request.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, looking at this, that's what we were doing all along. Have a look at our reports in 1993 and 1994, as well as 1995, because this is towards the end, in August 1995. This is precisely what we did. Date, frequency, azimuth, participants, et cetera. This may have been a circular letter which reminded all subordinate units that they need to harmonise the way they submitted reports. But this is what we followed throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted. And, I believe, after that we can go on our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2199, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I hear well when you said that you were recording everything, but once you realised a conversation was private, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Sometimes we recorded private conversations which did not contain any information but were of personal nature, say, an officer talked to his wife. We didn't think it was relevant for the command to know. Perhaps a conversation or two of that nature slipped by, but we usually never sent it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did the screening? Who made the selection of relevant as opposed to irrelevant conversations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Selection was usually made by the operator. He was aware of the contents and then perhaps consulted me or the squad leader or the computer operator. Sometimes such conversations were noted; sometimes they were not. Basically it all depended on the conversation itself, and we made a call right there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned me as well among those you listened to. Did you have such material; and did the OTP receive everything?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: As regards you, Mr. Karadzic, we did have recordings of your conversations. Among other things, you had particularly long conversations in 1995, in the summer and fall of that year, with certain representatives or sympathisers in London, Paris, Moscow, and you probably remember that. You also talked to other members of the Presidency, such as Koljevic, and who was it who came after you, with thick eyebrows?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, Krajisnik. Thank you. You also talked to many other people, starting with the General Staff and General Mladic, down to lower-ranking units who used that -- which used that type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Let me complete me answer. Because, in addition to asking whether we listened to your conversations, you asked me -- let me try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whether the OTP received all my conversations.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I don't know that. We sent conversations to the command, but I don't know how it was sorted, logged, archived, et cetera, or who received it in the end. That is something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you treat my conversations with my sympathisers, friends; and did you make a distinction between my conversations with -- my unofficial conversations as opposed to official conversations? Was there a selection made based on the collocutor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript. We did not carry out any selection. For the most part, all conversations of yours, Krajisnik's, Plavsic's, and Koljevic's, especially long conversations, well, there, they introduced themselves to you, and that's how we recorded them. I know that all those transcripts were in the notebooks, and the texts sent. I don't know whether they were all preserved and whether they will be used in this trial. Once we sent them on, our job was finished. We were no longer interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your personal impression. Do you agree that Serbs are not particularly skilled in keeping their secrets? In other words, were you able or did you have a feeling that you could receive and gain any information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Let me just wait for the transcript. You see, I have worked in communications for a long time, and I can say that the higher the rank or position, the less regard there is for the rules. So it was more difficult to eavesdrop on the lower-ranking units than it was on generals, because no one can say to a general what to say or not to say. That does not exist. They were prone to being less cautious the most. And I don't know who recommended it to them, probably the Army of Yugoslavia, that such communication was secure, but it wasn't true. There is no such thing as secure communication. In any case, they frequently said, when engaging in conversation, Talk freely. No one is listening in. So the most senior personnel were the least cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand well, then, that generals spoke freely and that they didn't only say things that were facts, but said other personal things, boasted, discussed many other things, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript again. I could observe, and it was particularly pronounced in the Orlovo theatre in 1993 -- well, I'm really sorry that we no longer have that material, but this would be particularly illustrative of your question. There were many JNA officers who came there to observe an exercise of sorts, and it was interesting to listen to their conversations when they called their colleagues in Belgrade and the way they discussed operations, what trenches they reached, and what lines they were. We forwarded all such information, and you could clearly see how they boasted of this and that. They bragged. And, for example, they had the intention of having an offensive at 7.00 p.m. that day, and thanks to the information we received, at 5.00 p.m. our forces engaged them in a counter-attack. And that was the end of their operation. Their objectives were clearly not met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it also happen that they said that today, for example, they had captured a hill which they were really intending to take the next day. Did they brag of -- about such things?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, you know, a lot of time has passed, so I can't be specific. But the conversations are in the notebooks. If you have time and interest, you may look it up and then obtain that information. I no longer can say anything specific in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't need you to be specific. You mentioned the boasting yourself. Did they sometimes talk of things in advance although such things did not take place at the time of conversation? Did they exaggerate things? Did they boast?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, yes, they would boast and exaggerate, especially on the Orlovo battle-field. As to whether they spoke about certain things prematurely in advance, I really don't know. But, yes, they would say they'd arrived here or there. They'll do this tomorrow, then that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that these conversations show that some of the participants were aware of the fact that their conversations were being intercepted? And they would ever say, Well, let the Turks listen to us. So did they reveal a fact that they were aware that they were being listened to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of my experience, according to the information that I had, up until the Autumn of 1995 they were convinced that we weren't listening to them. That's probably because they didn't know how they were being listened to and what equipment was being used for that purpose. But they did know that there were perhaps one or two radio relay devices that had remained in our territory, these centres, and it was probably on that basis that they came to the conclusion that we couldn't listen in to their conversations. And at the beginning of my testimony I said that what we did couldn't even have been done with the original equipment, radio relay equipment. You could have listened to one channel. It would not really have been adequate. The sort of interceptions that we made could not have been made with the original or old equipment, and we didn't really need this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do we agree that with regard to telephone communication hubs most of them remained on the Muslim side in Mostar, Sarajevo. I don't know whether there was anything in Livno, Tuzla, Zenica, Bihac. As far as telephone infrastructure is concerned, were the Serbs in a more disadvantageous position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, look, this is a civilian phone network that was in existence. It had been in existence for a number of years before the war. And I don't know -- we're discussing a military network here that the Drina Corps, with JNA equipment, managed to establish. They established a war-time communication network. But this other network was a civilian one, in Kladanj, Jovanovici, Tuzla. Well, each municipality or each post office, in fact, had its own radio relay system of a similar kind, because that was the latest technology at the time. And the radio relay equipment was obtained from Sweden. It wasn't local equipment. So I wouldn't compare those two types of networks. I wouldn't want to analyse whether someone was in a better position or in a more disadvantageous position. That's not really relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the war, was it customary for the sides involved to provide each other with misinformation? I think the witness is waiting for the letter A.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes, I'm waiting. But I can start giving you my answer. I personally don't know. My job wasn't to assess whether or not someone was involved in deception. My job and the task of my staff was as follows: What we heard, we'd have to record, transcribe, and forward. Someone else in the command was perhaps involved in these other tasks. I really don't know. But that wasn't our task, and we didn't perform any such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if on the basis of metacommunication, intonation, and so on and so forth, one came to the conclusion that the enemies were providing you with misinformation and saying that they were going to attack such and such a place but that wasn't their intention, in such cases would you inform your superiors of the fact? Would you inform them of the fact that you thought misinformation was being provided?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: We never got involved in such things. We never commented the conversations we recorded and forwarded. That was not our task, and that's not something that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any problems? I'm now referring to the beginning of July, the first half of July 1995. During that period in time did you have any problems with the equipment you had, with the way in which it functioned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in relation to the period you are asking me about, I don't think so. I think we performed our duties adequately, correctly, and I think that on the 13th of July, when Mr. Krstic issued orders about clearing the terrain and saying there were to be no survivors, I was with my colleague, sitting next to him. I heard that conversation live, the conversation that my colleague sitting next to me had recorded. So I know that everyone was working adequately at the time and we didn't have any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have any problems with the computers, with the level of confidentiality that was to be preserved for your work?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, as far as -- as confidentiality is concerned in relation to our work, no, we never had any problems. But as far as the equipment is concerned, as far as the computers are concerned, sometimes it was necessary to refresh the system, because the computers at the time were fairly old ones, fairly slow, so their memory capacity was not very significant. But that really wasn't a problem. Sometimes perhaps a file wouldn't be forwarded in time, but within two or three hours or in the course of the day it would be forwarded. And finally, we made a selection. We would only forward urgent files immediately. But less important files would be sent at the end of the report or once a certain number of reports had been accumulated. It's not as if whenever we'd recorded a conversation we would forward it, if it wasn't a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What exactly did Krstic say when you listened to him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Well, what was his rank? A colonel or lieutenant-colonel? Beara. It had to do with the clearing of the terrain after the 11th of September, after the Serbian forces had entered Srebrenica. On that occasion, the two of them had a conversation, and Beara submitted a report to Krstic and said that they were clearing the terrain, that things were going well. And finally Krstic told him, You know that there will be no survivors. He said, I know that, boss. That's what is being done. We have the authentic recording. You can listen to it, Mr. Karadzic. I didn't record that conversation, but I did hear it. So now on the basis of what I can remember I'm interpreting it. So perhaps I'm not a hundred per cent precise. But my colleague who recorded and transcribed it made a record and it can be found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D05204, please. It's the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says that you had problems and that a file was being sent again. So if you saw that something was not going well, you would repeat the action, which you wouldn't do if everything went well; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. Well, look, when you send a file, then the other side, the command to whom we were sending the file, if for some reason there was some mistakes in the file or if it hadn't been fully forwarded, they would then inform us of the fact that the file hadn't been received and then we would send the file again in the same form. But if it wasn't an urgent file -- well, if it was urgent, it meant it wouldn't arrive in time, and that was not good for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says at the top: As a reason -- for this reason we are sending to you the file in question. And then it gives a number. In what sense was the file referred to in question or problematic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a translation. I hope the participants have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm waiting for the interpretation to be completed. The file was problematic because in the command we were informed through Paket communications that they hadn't received the complete file. That is why the file was problematic. It hadn't been received, and that is why we sent it again. So it wasn't problematic in any other sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a document from the Prosecution but without this -- this note concerning the problematic nature -- without this complaint. And the remainder was admitted as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The remainder of the document, without the introduction, was admitted. It was tendered by the Prosecution, and I'm now tendering this with this additional complaint that refers to difficulties encountered when transmitting the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the number of the document that has been tendered by the Prosecution? Or, Mr. Costi, could you help us in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he's referring to 65 ter number 3 -- I'm sorry. 20807. Should be this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second then. Could we upload it. 20807.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Because this is the only document we tendered because it's discussed in amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think -- probably it may be one of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page. In that case, I would tender this as a document of ours. Can we see the next page. 1D05204.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, this is another document. We need -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll mark the previous document for identification because we didn't see the English translation. In the meantime, you may proceed. We'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see the name of -- of a place, and then we need to put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D2200, provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, and I'm not sure this is helpful. I couldn't -- I just got into this belatedly. I didn't know if you were looking for the exhibit number of the intercept that was tendered earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic said this is -- part of this document was admitted as Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, and I didn't know if you were looking for that particular exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in this -- I -- I saw that -- saw the place of a name [sic] in the previous document. That's why I suggested to put -- put it under seal. What was the number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI, D2200, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, purely for planning purpose, could I ask how much time more you would need to conclude your cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I will be to complete my cross-examination within two hours. I won't even need the two hours you allocated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, how -- from now on, how much long -- how much would you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should perhaps complete my cross-examination by noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us give it a try. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's no longer on the screen, this document I was interested in. But does it say, does it not, that he's looking for Muslims for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this here? K says -- it's the eighth line from the bottom. It says: "Make a list of all the Muslims who are fit for military service so that we can transfer them and use them for an exchange." And what you recorded is what you wrote down; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. I recorded that and I wrote that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D05208. Again, could it please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this, this remark concerning work with the SPKZ? Can you tell us what that is, SPKZ?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: SP I know; it's a type of software. It's a computer programme. And KZ is "encrypted." So it meant that it coded and decoded communication by way of digipeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what does it say here? In the second paragraph it says: It caught our interest and today we went a bit further. Namely, we reset the computer system date to the 9th of June and carried out the normal procedure for generating call-signs, and so on and so forth. And it said that today's date, the 8th of July, 1995, corresponds to the 9th of June in terms of call-signs and the chat mode used. And then the conclusion further down is that: "We believe that what we have found seriously jeopardizes the secrecy of work on PR and therefore we believe that responsible officials in the 2nd Corps ... should be made aware of this immediately." So that was a problem, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Yes. One of the problems that was not isolated. There were problems, as you can see here, but, after all, the operator down there who was better versed in this kind of communication than I was did his job and came to a conclusion. This just shows that my people were quite knowledgeable as far as these technical things were concerned, and now I really cannot recall how this problem was resolved, whether somebody brought in a better system, cassette, or whether the system was re-booted. I don't know. Within four or five hours a new computer could have arrived, or some other equipment. I mean, I do not know specifically now. I cannot say. But it did not really affect our work. We could have sent it with the date that the computer had recorded, but we knew what kind of a mistake it was and that it referred to another time. I don't think it is something that affected the regularity of our normal work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted. I wonder whether "primjedba" is translated properly by using the word "remark." I think that primjedba can also be translated as "objection." Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2201, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The Prosecution will undertake the exercise of redacting certain names of places and produce public versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will do -- the Defence do the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 20807. Could I have that, please. Again, could it please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the 8th of July, and now we are showing the document dated the 13th of July, and you'll probably remember that. I see. This has already been admitted under a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that day, on the 13th of July, it says that there was a computer problem. It says that the computer drive is barely alive, kept alive. Yesterday we had to refresh it several times with the NDD programme. So on the 12th and 13th you had computer problems; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness at all if he's not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, could you speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is evident from the report that that's the way it was; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has been admitted as part associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were asked, in another trial against a Muslim general, audio recordings were requested from a group of you? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Maybe my command was asked about this, but I have no idea. No one asked me for anything, nor could anybody have received anything from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did someone from the Bosnian Ministry of Defence, for the purposes of this court, for the defence of a Muslim general, did they ask for recordings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: After I was demobilised in 1996, in April, immediately in the beginning of April, apart from this Tribunal, no one ever asked me for anything in any form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about this Tribunal, or for the purposes of this Tribunal, or upon orders of this Court. Did the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina ask you for specific recordings that had to do with General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as you put this question to me, it looks as if I'm supposed to have some kind of private collection of these recordings, and I don't have any such thing. And there was no need for me to have that kind of thing. So he could not have asked me for that kind of thing. I mean, but he could have asked me, but he couldn't have received anything because I don't have any such thing. Once we completed the recording and the transcription and once the notebook and tape were sent to the command, I'd never see that again, except when I came here and when documents were shown to me, then I saw them. But as for the rest, I had no contact whatsoever with any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the ministry contact you, though, in relation to that? Did anybody talk to you about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: From our state, from our side, whatever you say, no one was really expressing any interest in our work. I mean, it was only the Tribunal. No one ever -- well, I mean, at least I'm talking about myself. I'm not speaking about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D05213. Can we have a look at that, please. Could it please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this. Ministry of Defence. It's the Ministry of Defence that is writing to this OTP, and they are referring to a letter in which they are being asked for co-operation, assistance in providing information, and there's a specific reference.
