And then it says that that was handed over, and that, obviously, they are repeating here as well that they did not contact you to ask whether there was anything else; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters were not able to hear you again. But, Mr. Costi, is there any reason not for broadcasting this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure about it. I -- I don't think so. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: -- let me get back on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I hear of this and see this. Perhaps these organs did contact someone. I mean, I see my own name and I see other names, other people. But I really have no idea about any of this. No one had ever contacted me. Perhaps someone provided something to someone else but then they did not consider it necessary. I mean, after all, we had never recorded any conversation here. I mean, the one that you're referring to here, about the general, about this General Delic. Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, Mr. President, I might state the obvious, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you say it's obvious. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that on the 22nd of July, 1995, the document that is under this number, the third bullet point here, where there is a reference to the names of the operators who intercepted the conversations, you claim that there was no intercepted conversation then?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not sure if this is what the witness actually said. I think he commented that he has no idea about the document. He didn't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me put it this way then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that it was established here, document number such and such, pertains to an intercepted conversation of General Delic's, and what is being asked for is that persons who intercepted that conversation should help in obtaining this, and the person's names are referred to here? So are you trying to say that there was no intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, again. I don't think he's trying to say that there wasn't a conversation. I think he said he has no idea about the document itself. I'm sorry to interrupt again, but it's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he can answer that question as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, see? I mean, I'm assuming what it was that had happened. Number 1, that's my name and surname, and it's stated that I'm a platoon commander. And since I've spent most of my time in the first department -- I mean, rather, this is the first department, and I was in the second department. And these are two persons who had completely different jobs, and it's possible that during their shift when I was not present they recorded that conversation. So then they should be asked about this. I'm just referred to here as the person in charge of that platoon. I mean, I am not familiar with this, and that's why I'm saying that I don't know about it. And, finally, well, yes, obviously this is a document -- well, yeah, it's clear. I mean, I personally don't know about this. But it's possible that these two men -- well, because the other one was the commander of this first group, and the other one was the other person who might have recorded that consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I'm interested in the following, and, of course, you cannot give an answer to this question, but why did the ministry not contact you? And why did they not ask for your assistance in this regard? So they didn't; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, he has already answered, but clearly this is call for speculation from the witness, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I mean, it was discussed by the witness. I'm not sure he provided basis for admission of this document. And I know other witnesses will come discussing the chain of custodies of all these intercepts, and might be the proper course of action, I think, going through those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not challenge the authenticity of this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated by Mr. Costi, we'll not admit this document through this witness. This witness didn't testify anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I should have objected before your decision. The witness testified that he had not been contacted. And we have this problem with Bosnia-Herzegovina that is not co-operating, and avoiding giving any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have another opportunity to tender this document through another channel, other witnesses who can testify --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to this, or through a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MFI D2024, could we now have that. D2024, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can this please not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- do you recognise the document; and is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Karadzic, this is not my handwriting. And this is not a document that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the designations? Is it from your location? What is this 7-8 -- well, the figure there.

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: 785 is the frequency of the radio relay station. 785 megahertz. 1305 is the hour. Based on the text alone, I can't say where it's from. You need to show me the file in the computer and then we can see based on that. So notebooks were working material frequently without the date, only frequency and time. That is to say, the things relevant for the typing up in the computer. This was quite regular in notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 35027, page 84. I believe it was presented by the Prosecution, but I'd like us to see page 85 in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go down the page. Page 85 -- 84 in e-court and in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look. Is this the usual way how it was transcribed, especially where it says "Karadzic," here, give me the command post at Kusic's?

utterances.speaker: KDZ245
utterances.text: I can see it, yes. It seems that you are speaking. Karadzic is here. Give me the command post at Kusic's. So you introduced yourself to Kusic. Well, now it's gone. Put General Mladic on the phone. And then the answer is: General Mladic is away. Then you seem to say: Very well. Tell Mladic that I approved UNHCR participation in Karakaj in the evacuation of population. So you wanted them to tell Mladic you had approved their participation in the evacuation of civilians in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this the usual way it was noted down, and was it noted down literally? Or is it an interpretation? Is it direct speech or simply an interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was a commander of a platoon and then he can answer as far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that this is not my handwriting. Mr. Karadzic did not even ask me whether this transcript was mine. She [as interpreted] wanted me to read it, and I did. It contains sufficient information that the operator who recorded it could sit behind a computer and type it, because in the computer there is the reference to the unit and other data, such as the date. In notebooks, for the most part, you will find conversations recorded in this fashion without a date. It was working material. You asked me in my testimony if we would do it differently. If we were to do it again, we would try to put all information in, including first and last names, but this is how we worked at the time, and it was enough. What is important is what was noted down. utterances.speaker: KDZ245

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave it at that time. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. I would now like -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to now read a short summary of the witness testimony. During the war, the witness served as a member of an intercept unit of the ABiH. He was assigned to the northern facility as a commander of a squad of intercept operators. The witness in his testimony described the equipment they used and the standard procedure they applied in their job. He explained that they would scan, monitor, the frequencies and directions provided by the command, with an order. And once they picked up a sign or a sound, they would stop the scanning and start to record. Conversation considered interesting would be transcribed in a working notebook. From there, the conversation was then typed into a computer and sent to the command. When transcribing the conversation in the notebook, the witness and his squad listened to the tape in small sections in order to be accurate. If part of the conversation was inaudible, was unclear, they would put dots or leave a blank section. And if they were not hundred percent sure of one word, they would write the same word and a question mark. Similarly, if they did not know the name of the speaker, they would use a dash, indicate the speaker as X, Y, or a number. No change was made once the intercept was transcribed in the working notebook. The witness explain that it was in their interest to be accurate and precise, since the conversation was intercepted because they were important for them at that time. The witness further identifies his handwriting on several pages and discussed several intercepts. This, Your Honours, ends my -- my brief summary. And we do not have any question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, whenever you feel necessary -- feel it's necessary to take a break, please don't hesitate to let us know. And your evidence in-chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and, as you noticed, now you will be further asked by the Defence, Mr. Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand that. But could I ask you to make a correction here. I don't know whether it's an error that slipped in when the statement was typed out, but there is a mistake in the statement. In one part it says a platoon commander, but it was the commander of a detachment, not of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I may have -- I may have said erroneously "platoon." If I said it, I meant "squad commander." This is what is said, I believe, in the statement. But I'm going to check in the statement whether there is also a mistake in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Witness, what Mr. Prosecutor has read out does not form of evidence. What is evidence is what you stated in your statement. So rest assured. Thank you for your clarification. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness, sir.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you completed your electromechanical school -- what was it called?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: It was called a school for electromechanics.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to -- to interrupt, but I suppose these are information that should remain -- should be said in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us, sir, is it correct that as you yourself said you were mobilised by the secretariat for information and propaganda in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes. The secretariat -- that secretariat mobilised me there to my first position in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is a civilian authority body; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We should both make pauses between question and answer, if possible, to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Could they have mobilised you prior to the declaration of a state of war? Was that legal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about the laws. I was mobilised, as far as I can remember, on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak up or to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this was in accordance with the laws or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone so that you can speak into the microphone. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it was legal or not, in accordance with the laws or not, I don't know. But I do know that I received an appeal. I reported to the duties that I had been asked to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you do prior to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I worked in my company prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite sufficient. Do you remember that a state of war was declared on the 20th of June, and you were mobilised before that date, on the 14th of June? You were transferred to military department. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, but that was in the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you for that clarification. Do you remember that war was declared on the 20th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date, but I assume that it was around that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the task that this municipal secretariat had to perform in your municipality? We won't mention the name of the municipality. I'm not sure that such things existed in all municipalities. When was this secretariat established and what was its task?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I can't say anything about the tasks of the secretariat for information and propaganda. All I can tell you about concerns the duties that I had to perform within that secretariat. My job consisted of the following: I had to help the way the television network functioned in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, up until June 1993, you weren't involved in the work that you were subsequently involved in with these interception devices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period of time, you lived in your municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly move into private session in case -- the name of the municipality should not be revealed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it true that your town is in the depth of the territory? It's not, in fact, on the actual front line.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the beginning of the war about a thousand, around 900-odd, Serbs were kept at the stadium and they were maltreated there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, did you observe, that the centre we mentioned in private session was turned into a prison, and a certain number of Serbs were held in detention there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I know that part of that centre was turned into a prison. And it's not just that a certain number of Serbs were detained there, but some members of the Territorial Defence were also detained there for various errors they had committed or various misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many Serbs were there in your municipality, let's, say, in 1993? And how many Serbs are there in your municipality today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, I can't really provide you with such information. I can't really tell you how many of them there were in 1993. In any event, there are fewer of them there now than there were in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we agree that there are far fewer of them now? The census shall be carried out very soon.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: The census will show what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, where were the Serbs in your municipality? Where did they live, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I don't know where they went. Many Muslims went. Many Croats left as well, to various parts of the world. In my municipality, there are many Muslims of -- who are now in America, in the Netherlands, who are in countries all over the world. I also have Serb friends who are all over the world, and I still have contact with them to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did a lot of Muslims really leave your municipality as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why. It's not Serbian territory, it wasn't at the concentration line, so in that case why did the Muslims leave and go to other places throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, why? I can just provide you with one example. At the beginning of the war, many people sent their families, their women and children, wherever possible. And later, when they established contact, the others left too. In other words, the families would be reunited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether there's any specific reasons for you not to start with issues relating to intercepts? Otherwise, given the limited time, I would like you focus on those more critical issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I will keep my promise to complete my cross-examination today. But we seldom have the opportunity to listen to a decent man from a Muslim background who will testify to what he experienced and saw, and this is certainly something that will be of assistance to the Chamber. Very well. We will now move on to other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one other question. The number of the Serbs diminished. What about the number of Muslims? Did it increase or diminish, and where did they go?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, I can't provide you with any concrete information, but I can express what my opinion is. It's a town that I live in, after all. I think the number of the Muslims increased. The number of Muslims from Srebrenica, Bratunac, and other places increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did they start arriving in (redacted) Was it immediately prior to the war -- immediately prior to the war? Did some people leave and some arrive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Not immediately prior to the war. It was around 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak up a little bit. The interpreter is having trouble hearing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Either you could come closer to the microphone or speak up a bit louder. The interpreters seem to have difficulty in following you. Thank you, sir. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Costi do we need a redaction at line 11 or line 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Where the name of municipality was cited. And, yeah, I was about to stand up and mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about the reasons for which you are here, the main reason for your presence here. In your statement, on page 2, paragraph 6, you said that you intercepted communications at the level of the VRS Corps and you deciphered or decrypted these communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: That's not what I said. We did intercept conversations. We recorded them on a tape and then we transcribed them in a log-book. But there was a different service that was involved in decryption. It was in the room next to our room. They were very close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When I said that, I had your service, your department in mind, not yourself personally. So you could decrypt encrypted communications at the level of VRS Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, is there something that I could correct here? When I record a conversation and transcribe it in a notebook, I then handed the conversation over. It would be typed out. And that is where my work finished. I don't know what would subsequently be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the summary, you said that you received orders. Does this mean that you worked in accordance with the orders from the army and for the benefit of the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of the ordering process and issuing of tasks, did any court or judicial organ take part in it, such as an investigating judge or someone else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I received orders from my platoon commander. I don't know who he received his orders from. I suppose from his company commander or someone higher up. In any case, I received my orders from him or, in his absence, from the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the channels and levels and participants were determined -- well, what was it that your superior command determined? What was it that they ordered and that you could not change?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Orders I received always included antenna position, frequency - and this goes for the RRU-800 device. So we received an order containing the direction, such as south-east, and frequency. Then we would turn our antennae and scan the channels which were pre-set in the device. If there was any communication, we recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many channels did the RRU-800 have, and what was the distance it can cover, the range?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: The RRU-800 had a maximum of 24 channels. As for its range, I don't know that. It wasn't part of my job. I was just an operator involved in the technical part of the whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the interpretation, and I would kindly ask to you do the same.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the scanner picked up something or when you would hear that there was some activity on a particular channel, you stopped the scanning process and returned to the channel in question in order to record.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, was it customary or understood that you would lose the very beginning of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: It all depended on when we registered a conversation on a particular channel. Sometimes we could even get to the very beginning of the conversation; whereas, sometimes we could get to that channel towards the end of the conversation, sometimes in the middle. It all depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you under an obligation to identify the participants and to send information to your users, to your commands, about the participants?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: If the participants could be identified, we did that. If not, we didn't identify them. Then we would put a dash or an X or a letter, depending on the number of participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you identify them? Did you wait until they introduced themselves, or did you apply certain recognition methods?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I can only discuss my work and the work of my shift. What was the method of recognition? We identified participants according to the way they introduced themselves. It rarely happened, although it did happen, that we would recognise people. But it happened seldom. I don't know how to explain that. When you have been listening to a voice for a few days and you recognise the tone modulations. Or, for example, when I speak to my wife on the phone, the moment I hear her voice I know it's her, if you understand my point. But this did happen seldom. Usually the participants introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the way of decoding and the codes used by the VRS at corps level?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I really can't say anything about that. That was not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you, and with what devices, locate the participants? Could you tell where they were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: My job was not to locate the participants. Once I received an order, I had to implement it. It meant turning the antenna and operate the device. I had to duly work and scan and record and then transfer into a notebook correctly. Another service was in charge of identifying, so I really can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the working or frequency range of the RRU-800?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, the frequency range, I don't know it off the cuff. But between 600 and 800 megahertz, I think. Once I left that position, I no longer worked with such matters, so I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the RRU-1? How many channels and what is the frequency range?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the RRU-1 worked between 180 and 300 megahertz. It did not have channels. It scanned in terms of frequency volume. It simply went up and down the frequency range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that besides recording there was also a noting down of conversations live?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you and your soldiers write down conversations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Do you mean without any recording?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Instead of recording.

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: In my shift, that never happened. We had a procedure in place that we had to abide by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the other shifts, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss other shifts. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the first half of July 1995. Were you in the facility beginning with O?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I think I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of communication did you follow? Only Serbs? Or Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: At that time, we monitored only one RRU-800 direction, as well as RRU-1, which was the Serb direction or channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the frequencies used for the communication of members of the 28th Division? And did you record any of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So any electronic insight you could have of events in and around Srebrenica in the course of those few days came solely based on the communication of the Serb army; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, and in what way, learn about the decision for the 28th Division not to surrender but to fight its way out to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I have never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By listening to Serb radio traffic, could you see what the intensity of fighting was and the number of losses in that period?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: You see, a lot of time has passed. While I was up there, while I listened to some conversations, I was appalled. I couldn't believe what was being done. But, now, 17 years later, I really can no longer recall some of the things, especially if I did not work on them directly. I can't even remember many things that I worked on, which is quite a normal thing after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of your work, could you monitor my communication with someone? And do you recall anything of that sort that you recorded or wrote down?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I recall a conversation which involved you and an intermediary. However, there were also many cases when I was not at work when your conversations were intercepted. However, I was not involved in that, so I can't say anything about it. You should ask the person who intercepted it and recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you discussing the conversation on the 13th of March, at some time, between the late Miroslav Deronjic and myself through an intermediary? Was that the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just wonder whether Mr. Karadzic got the date wrong, because I believe it wasn't the 13 of March. That conversation was discussed in other session in this court before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we discuss it in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But I -- probably it's a type or misspelling, misspoke of 13th of July, not March. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. My eyes fooled me. Because I know that on the 13th of March the witness corrected something which has to do with the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to a conversation in which Deronjic and I could not communicate directly as we could not hear each other; it all went through an intermediary who conveyed his messages to me and the other way around? Is that the only conversation involving me that you recorded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that lately you have corrected your previous statement, where you said you thought I was in the same room with the intermediary; whereas, in the notebook --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sorry to step in. I would like to see the cite for the witness saying that -- that he was in the same room. I don't think this was said by the witness, as far as I recall. But if you could get a cite, maybe that clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have a look at 65 ter 31036C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that intercept: [In English] "The intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room." [Interpretation] Could we have a look at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you withdraw your objection, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I believe my objection was about the cite, and I'm not sure whether the witness ever testified about that. He's reading an intercept and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, right. So, for clarity, why don't we upload it and let's show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that's not it. Can we see the page following this one? Just one moment. A and C. In the printed intercept, it says C. Actually, can we have a proofing note, 1D05199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see it on page 4 in English. And it's 2010 hours. So in B/C/S ... page 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to make clear, my -- Mr. Karadzic said, at page 81, lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Perfect. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're -- we see here, in the parentheses, "Intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you made a correction in the proofing note two days ago?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: As for the typed version, I don't want to discuss it at all. I'd like to see the original, the handwriting version, the one I noted down by listening to the tape. And then we can compare it with this one. I didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, given your profession: Would it have made sense to be in the same room with the intermediary and let him listen to the collocutor and convey my words, or would it have been more logical to conclude that both I and the other participant were far aware and we had no direct means of communication?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss the text before me. I would like to see my own transcript, and that is what I can discuss. If possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Then we're going to take a look and see whether we have it here. Just a moment, please. I think that it could be 65 ter 31036. Does the content sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you did record this; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 31036A. Let us not have this broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this familiar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: This is very familiar. As you can see, up here it is not written at all that you were sitting in a common room. This is what I wrote, and this is the only thing that I can discuss, and I do not wish to discuss other matters. Now, why it is written the way it is written over there, that is not my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it could happen that something that exists in the typewritten version is not in the handwritten version; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, well, perhaps I should put it this way: that in the typewritten version there are things that are not in the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the handwritten version be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's already admitted as part of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will do as well. But I meant because of the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You meant to tender that proofing note? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. That's about the third time. The witness has not made any correction to his statement, as keeps being put to him. The witness noticed a discrepancy between the handwritten version and the printout. That is not the witness making a correction to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's clear, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then have 1D05199. I find this confusing. If he hadn't corrected it, how can the proofing note ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not that he corrected. He indicated the discrepancy. We will see. We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: [As read] Participated in the proofing and [In English] witness made the following comment about intercept A and C. The printout intercept 31036C indicates in the heading that the intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room, while the notebook version he wrote ... does not have the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this proofing note, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, whether it's necessary, I'm not sure. But I don't see any problem in admitting this. Yes, we'll give number. And we'll put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2203, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you get the impression, or, rather, did you have any insight, did you talk to your colleagues, about the level of fighting, the level of losses during that week? Between Srebrenica and Kalesija, Srebrenica and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, if you were to have the same task again, would you propose certain changes in the methodology involved; and if, so what would you suggest should be improved?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Well, that's a relative question. If I had the same task, you know what I'd change? The only thing that I would change, I'd issue an order to my men to write very, very legibly and clearly. That would be number one. I have to tell you that everything that we recorded and everything that we received, we did all of that to help the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, our own command. Not at any point in time could I have imagined that it would have come to where it is now. If I were to be doing this again, we would strictly pay attention to that, because probably we would assume that this would arrive here. And then I would have kept the notebooks and the tapes and everything in order to make all of this easier. That's the only thing I would change, from the point of view of my own job and the tasks involved in my job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case, if it were to be used by a court of law and for those purposes it would have been more complete and more accurate. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague get again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank this Court. And I am very pleased if I managed to be of any assistance to have this case resolved in a positive or in a negative sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Just one -- we discussed about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let us wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we submit that this particular intercept we just discussed should be admitted into evidence right now. The reason being that -- we are fully aware that 89(C) requires the evidence to be of probative value and also relevant, but I would say there is no real discussion here as whether this evidence is relevant or not. The relevance is it appears quite clear and it was discussed to full extent, which is Mr. Karadzic's involvement in the events of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't dispute the relevance of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking about more some comprehensive resolution, but given the situation, we'll admit this in ... in full. 65 ter 31036. Shall we continue, or shall we adjourn for the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the latter, Mr. President. I think the timing came as a surprise to everyone, including VWU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume tomorrow -- no, next week, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the morning, at 9.00. And we'll start with KDZ357. Bonne weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.08 p.m.,
